strengths: The paper addresses a relevant NLP safety problem: harmful content can occur in exposed reasoning traces even when final answers appear safer. Evaluating reasoning and final answers separately is a useful contribution.

The training-free combination of attention-guided intervention and attention-based trajectory selection is practically motivated. The paper provides equations, pseudocode, the intervention text, and several component and hyperparameter ablations.

The reported safety improvements are substantial across several settings. For example, on R1-Llama-8B under H-CoT, Table 2 reports reductions in AdvBench harmfulness from 86%/52% to 2%/2% for reasoning/final answers.

The evaluation covers five models, multiple attack families, seven defenses, general capability benchmarks, over-refusal, and inference efficiency. General benchmark accuracy is largely preserved on average, although individual settings show losses.
weaknesses: The central claim of mitigating exaggerated safety is contradicted by important results in Table 11. On safe XSTest queries, R1-Qwen-7B final-answer full compliance falls from 92% without defense to 26%, while full refusal rises from 4% to 56%. R1-Llama-8B full compliance falls from 100% to 58%, and R1-Qwen-32B from 98% to 70%. Improvements over some restrictive baselines do not establish that over-refusal is avoided. The treatment of partial refusals in F1 also needs an explicit formula: some high reasoning F1 scores coexist with predominantly partial-refusal outputs.

The decoding procedure is insufficiently specified for reliable reproduction. Equations use attention from layer l without identifying the selected layer or aggregation across layers. Sink identification requires attention from subsequently generated tokens, but Algorithm 1 begins with encoding the input and omits the required lookahead generation, rollback, and cache handling. It also places the start of reasoning after </think>. The second-sink stopping rule, its search interval, and how the claimed Wmax bound is enforced need an executable specification.

Experimental reproducibility and uncertainty reporting are inadequate. Appendix B.5 acknowledges random dataset subsets and quantization of some models without specifying all subset sizes and identities, sampling seeds, affected models, or quantization configurations. Sampling parameters and generation limits are also missing. AdvBench uses only 50 queries, and results lack repeated runs or confidence intervals, limiting confidence in smaller differences and reported zero failure rates.

The evidence for the proposed attention mechanism is suggestive rather than conclusive. Similar marginal distributions of human and detected transition positions in Figure 3 do not demonstrate per-example localization accuracy. Human evaluation provides mean scores without sample counts or inter-annotator agreement. Figure 4 reports top-3 agreement with oracle-best paths, whereas deployment selects one path; random-selection and tie-aware controls are missing. A matched comparison of IAS selection against random or likelihood-based selection would better isolate its contribution beyond safety prompting and additional candidates.

The robustness claims exceed the tested threat model. The described attacks are generated for each model, but the paper does not establish that attackers optimize against the active defense. H-CoT prompts are manually reconstructed without a sufficiently reproducible prompt collection. Several substantial residual failures also qualify the broad claims: Table 2 reports 52% final-answer fulfillment for R1-Llama-8B under PAIR on SorryBench, and Table 9 reports 50% final-answer harmfulness for QwQ-32B under PAIR on AdvBench.

The efficiency evidence supports a narrower conclusion than the stated total-cost claims. ATGR measures average time per generated token; a 7–9% increase does not directly establish the same increase in end-to-end latency when output lengths and discarded candidate computation differ. Table 5 reports token consumption, but a clear accounting of all candidate tokens, attention extraction, and request-level latency is needed. Overall, the promising safety gains warrant revision, but the unresolved central-claim and reproducibility issues prevent a sound Findings recommendation at present.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant NLP safety problem: harmful content in exposed reasoning traces as well as final answers. Its training-free combination of attention-guided intervention and candidate-path selection is a concrete, potentially useful contribution.

The experiments cover five reasoning models, seven defenses, three attack methods, and separate evaluations of reasoning and final answers. Several improvements are substantial: on R1-Qwen-32B under H-CoT, Table 2 reports reductions from 86%/56% harmfulness without defense to 4%/2%.

The paper includes utility benchmarks, over-refusal evaluation, timing measurements, component ablations, and human assessment of intervention locations. These provide useful evidence beyond attack-success rates alone.
weaknesses: The central claim of mitigating exaggerated safety is contradicted by substantial portions of Table 11. On benign XSTest queries, R1-Qwen-7B final-answer full compliance falls from 92% to 26%, while full refusal rises from 4% to 56%. For R1-Llama-8B, compliance falls from 100% to 58%; for R1-Qwen-32B, from 98% to 70%. ReasoningGuard also underperforms ThinkingI on final-answer F1 for several models. The treatment of partial refusals in F1 is insufficiently specified, making high reasoning-side F1 scores difficult to interpret. These results require a materially more qualified safety–utility claim.

The inference procedure is insufficiently specified for reliable reproduction. Sink identification requires attention from subsequent generated tokens, but Algorithm 1 encodes only the input before accessing these positions; lookahead generation, truncation, and cache handling are not explained. It also identifies the start of reasoning as occurring after </think>. The attention layer, window advancement, precise candidate-generation procedure, and implementation of second-sink detection are unclear. These details affect both the method and its claimed computational bound.

Experimental reproducibility and uncertainty reporting are inadequate. Appendix B.5 acknowledges randomly sampled evaluation subsets and quantization for certain models without identifying all subset sizes, sampled examples, seeds, or model-specific quantization settings. The 50-query AdvBench evaluation is small, and no confidence intervals or repeated-run variability are provided. Manually reconstructed H-CoT prompts and missing SafeDecoding expert-model details further limit reproducibility and confidence in baseline comparisons.

Evidence for the proposed attention mechanism is suggestive rather than decisive. Similar marginal distributions of human and automatic transition positions in Figure 3 do not establish per-example localization accuracy. Human evaluation lacks agreement statistics and comparative ratings for alternative locations. Figure 4 reports top-3 matching against oracle-selected paths, whereas deployment selects a single highest-IAS path; random-selection controls and tie handling are needed. Table 1 and Figure 5 provide useful ablations, but do not cleanly isolate IAS ranking from extra sampling under matched compute and intervention text.

The robustness claims exceed the demonstrated threat model. The evaluation does not clearly establish that attacks were optimized against the defended system. Residual vulnerabilities are also substantial: Table 2 reports 52% final-answer fulfillment for R1-Llama-8B under PAIR on SorryBench, and Table 9 reports 50% final-answer harmfulness for QwQ-32B under PAIR on AdvBench. These results support improvement against selected attacks, not consistently strong protection.

The reported 7–9% overhead is an average token-generation-time ratio, not a direct measure of end-to-end latency or total computation. Branch generation, discarded lookahead, attention extraction, memory use, and execution parallelism need clearer accounting. Table 5's changing output lengths further complicate translating ATGR into deployment cost.

Overall, the positive safety results warrant revision rather than dismissal, but unresolved reproducibility issues and contradictory evidence for a central safety–utility claim prevent a sound Findings recommendation in the current form. These appear addressable through clarified implementation, corrected claims, and targeted additional evaluation, supporting resubmission next cycle.

strengths: The paper addresses an important NLP safety problem: harmful content can appear in exposed reasoning traces even when final answers appear safe. Evaluating reasoning and final answers separately is a useful contribution.

ReasoningGuard combines attention-guided intervention timing with attention-based continuation selection in a training-free framework. The approach is practically motivated and goes beyond inserting a safety reminder at the beginning of generation.

The reported safety improvements are substantial across several settings. For example, on R1-Llama-8B under H-CoT, Table 2 reports reductions from 86%/52% to 2%/2% unsafe reasoning/final answers on AdvBench.

The evaluation includes five models, seven defenses, multiple safety evaluators, utility benchmarks, and component ablations. Tables 3 and 7 provide encouraging evidence that aggregate performance on conventional knowledge and reasoning tasks is largely preserved.
weaknesses: The central claim of avoiding exaggerated safety is contradicted by important results in Table 11. On benign XSTest prompts, final-answer full compliance falls from 92% to 26% for R1-Qwen-7B and from 100% to 58% for R1-Llama-8B; full refusal rises to 56% and 34%, respectively. For R1-Qwen-14B/32B, ThinkingI also achieves higher final-answer F1 than ReasoningGuard. These results require a substantially more qualified safety–utility claim. The treatment of partial refusals in F1 is unclear: R1-Qwen-14B receives reasoning F1 of 1.00 despite 76% partial refusal on safe inputs and 100% partial refusal on unsafe inputs.

Core implementation details are insufficient for reliable reproduction. The attention layer used in Equations 2 and 5 is unspecified. Sink detection requires attention from future generated tokens, but the generation, rollback, and cache-handling procedure is not explained. Algorithm 1 obtains attention by encoding the input and then uses positions in the output; it also identifies the closing </think> token as the start of reasoning. The second-sink stopping rule and the relationship between top-k branching and the stated greedy evaluation protocol need explicit specification.

The experimental setup leaves substantial uncertainty. Appendix B.5 acknowledges randomly sampled benchmark subsets and quantization for some models without specifying all subset sizes, sampled instances, seeds, or quantization configurations. Decoding settings and the manually reconstructed H-CoT prompts are not fully documented. There are no confidence intervals or repeated-run estimates; with only 50 AdvBench queries, small percentage differences should not support strong ranking claims.

Evidence for the proposed attention mechanism is suggestive rather than conclusive. Similar marginal distributions of human and detected transition positions in Figure 3 do not establish accurate per-example localization. Human evaluation reports average ratings without sample counts, inter-annotator agreement, or comparison against alternative locations. Figure 4 evaluates top-3 agreement with oracle paths, whereas deployment selects one path, and provides no random-selection reference or clear tie handling. Matched-budget controls using random timing and random continuation selection would better isolate the contribution of the attention signals.

The robustness claim exceeds the demonstrated threat model. The paper does not establish that attacks were optimized against the complete defended system. Moreover, meaningful residual failures remain: Table 2 reports 52% final-answer fulfillment under PAIR on SorryBench for R1-Llama-8B, and Table 9 reports 50% final-answer unsafety under PAIR on AdvBench for QwQ-32B. These outcomes warrant explicit failure analysis rather than broadly describing failures as rare or potentially evaluator false positives.

The efficiency evidence supports a narrower conclusion than the claimed minimal inference cost. ATGR measures time per generated token, not end-to-end latency or total compute, and refusal changes output length substantially. The paper does not clearly account for discarded branches, lookahead and recomputation, attention extraction, or memory costs. The asserted adaptive-budget bound also depends on a second-sink detection procedure that is not sufficiently defined. Overall, the promising safety results merit revision, but unresolved reproducibility issues and the unsupported over-refusal claim prevent a sound Findings recommendation in the current version.

The training-free combination of attention-guided intervention and attention-based continuation selection is technically interesting and applicable across several open model families.
Reported safety improvements are substantial. Table 3 shows large reductions relative to undefended models and competitive performance against both training-based and training-free safeguards.

The evaluation includes multiple attacks, utility benchmarks, over-refusal measurements, and ablations of intervention location, phrase composition, and sampling budget. These provide useful initial evidence beyond isolated examples.
weaknesses: The central claim of avoiding exaggerated safety is contradicted by important results. In Table 21, R1-Qwen-7B's full compliance on safe final answers falls from 96% to 54%, while full refusal rises from 2% to 36%. Table 22 reports reasoning F1 of 1.00 despite only 32% full compliance on safe queries and 96% partial refusal on unsafe queries. The handling of partial refusals in F1 needs explicit clarification; this metric does not establish the claimed safety–utility balance. Utility losses also include an 8.4-point MATH500 drop for R1-Qwen-7B.

The decoding procedure is insufficiently specified for reliable reproduction. Sink identification requires future generated tokens, but Algorithm 1 only encodes the input before accessing their attention and incorrectly locates reasoning after </think>. Buffering, rollback, continuation after selection, sliding-window advancement, and the precise second-sink stopping rule are missing. These details also determine whether the claimed O(kWmax) overhead bound holds.

Evaluation reproducibility and statistical support are inadequate. Appendix B specifies 50 AdvBench queries but describes other evaluations only as randomly sampled subsets, without complete sizes, identifiers, or seeds. Nucleus-sampling parameters, generation limits, and repeated-run uncertainty are not supplied. Consequently, small differences and claims of superiority over nine safeguards are difficult to assess.

The evidence for the proposed attention mechanism is weaker than claimed. Similar marginal distributions of human and detected transition positions do not demonstrate per-example localization accuracy; annotation counts and inter-annotator agreement are absent. Figure 4 measures top-three agreement although deployment selects the top-one path. Appendix C also conditions analysis on batches containing harmful outputs. These observations support an empirical association, not the stated sufficient condition for safety. Random or likelihood-based selection from identical candidates would better isolate IAS's contribution.

The claimed 5–9% inference-time overhead is based on average token generation time, not end-to-end request latency. Output lengths change substantially, and accounting for discarded branches, buffering, attention extraction, batching, and memory is unclear. Table 8's unlimited-budget variant uses over three times the tokens while reporting ATGR of only 1.10, illustrating why this metric alone cannot establish small total overhead.

Robustness claims exceed the demonstrated threat model. The paper does not clearly establish that attacks were optimized against the complete defended system. Some attacks are already weak against undefended models, while Appendix Table 20 still reports 70.5% final-answer fulfillment for AutoRAN against defended R1-Qwen-14B. Automated safety judgments also lack human calibration for reasoning traces. Overall, the promising empirical contribution needs methodological clarification, reproducible evaluation, and narrower claims before a sound Findings recommendation.

strengths: The paper addresses an important NLP safety problem: harmful content in exposed reasoning traces as well as final answers. Combining attention-guided intervention with inference-time trajectory selection is a concrete, potentially useful contribution.

The reported safety improvements are substantial across several model families and attack settings. For example, Table 3 reduces R1-Llama-8B’s average reasoning/final-answer harmfulness rates from 26.1/41.8 to 0.4/5.7. Comparisons include relevant training-based and training-free defenses.

The evaluation extends beyond attack success to utility, over-refusal, computational cost, phrase variants, and quantization. The appendices provide useful baseline configurations, qualitative examples, and a failure case.
weaknesses: The claimed mitigation of exaggerated safety is contradicted by important results. In Table 21, R1-Qwen-7B’s full compliance on safe final answers falls from 96% without defense to 54%, while full refusal rises from 2% to 36%; its F1 falls from 0.81 to 0.64. Table 22 reports reasoning F1 of 1.00 for R1-Qwen-14B despite 68% partial refusal on safe inputs and 96% partial refusal on unsafe inputs. The treatment of partial refusals in F1 needs an explicit definition and justification. These results require a substantially more qualified safety–utility claim.

The central decoding procedure is insufficiently specified for reliable reproduction. Algorithm 1 obtains attention by encoding the query, then uses attention from subsequently generated reasoning tokens without specifying the necessary lookahead, truncation, and cache handling. It also places the start of reasoning after </think>, apparently a consequential typo. The second-sink detection procedure, window advancement, and termination rules are unclear, although the adaptive-budget complexity claim depends on them. Appendix C uses B=160 and calls this aligned with the main experiments, whereas the main text emphasizes an adaptive budget bounded by Wmax=25.

Experimental uncertainty and reproducibility remain inadequate. Appendix B.5 acknowledges randomly sampled benchmark subsets, but their sizes and identities are not consistently specified, and sampling seeds, nucleus-decoding parameters, and generation limits are missing. Attack evaluation uses only 50 AdvBench queries. Without repeated runs or confidence intervals, small differences and zero observed failures do not establish reliable superiority. The broad improvements are promising, but the precise rankings need stronger support.

The attention-based explanation exceeds the evidence. Similar distributions of human and predicted transition positions in Figure 3 do not establish agreement for individual examples; paired localization errors and annotator agreement are needed. The IAS analysis selects batches containing harmful continuations, and Figure 4 reports top-three matching although deployment selects the top-one path. These analyses support a heuristic association, not the claim that high IAS is a sufficient condition for safety or that a safety scaling law has been established.

The efficiency claim conflates per-token time with total inference cost. ATGR measures average token generation time, whereas the method generates multiple candidate prefixes and requires attention access and lookahead. Table 8 itself shows that total token consumption and ATGR can behave quite differently. End-to-end latency, candidate-token accounting, batching, memory use, and the attention implementation are needed to substantiate the headline 5–9% overhead.

The robustness and utility conclusions need narrower wording. It is unclear whether attacks are optimized against the deployed defense or transferred from undefended models; the reported evaluation therefore does not establish adaptive robustness. Utility losses are also material in some settings: R1-Qwen-7B’s MATH500 accuracy drops from 92.9 to 84.5, and R1-Llama-8B’s GPQA accuracy drops from 52 to 44. Overall, the promising empirical contribution merits revision, but unresolved implementation details and unsupported central claims prevent a sound Findings recommendation at present.

strengths: The paper addresses an important NLP safety problem: harmful content in exposed reasoning traces, even when final answers appear safe. Evaluating reasoning and final answers separately is a meaningful strength.

ReasoningGuard combines attention-guided intervention timing with attention-based selection of short continuations, offering a practical training-free approach. Table 3 reports substantial safety improvements across multiple attacks; for R1-Qwen-7B, average reasoning/final-answer harmfulness metrics decrease from 32.9/46.4 to 0.3/4.6.

The evaluation covers several model families, nine principal defense baselines, utility benchmarks, and over-refusal tests. Intervention-location comparisons, phrase variants, sampling ablations, and additional guard-model comparisons provide useful supporting evidence.
weaknesses: The central claim of mitigating exaggerated safety is not consistently supported. In Table 21, R1-Qwen-7B's full compliance on safe final answers drops from 96% to 54%, while full refusal rises from 2% to 36%. Its final-answer F1 falls from 0.81 to 0.64. Moreover, F1 over FC and FR does not adequately explain treatment of partial refusals: R1-Llama-8B achieves reasoning F1 of 0.97 despite 62% partial refusal on safe queries. These results require a more qualified safety–utility claim and an explicit metric definition. Utility losses are also nontrivial in some settings, including MATH500 accuracy decreasing from 92.9 to 84.5 on R1-Qwen-7B.

Important implementation details remain unresolved. Algorithm 1 obtains attention by encoding the input but immediately uses attention from subsequently generated reasoning tokens, omitting the required lookahead generation and rollback. It also incorrectly locates the start of reasoning after </think>. The second-sink search and stopping rule, continuation after selecting a short path, and distinction between top-k token branching and sampling k trajectories need precise specification. These affect both reproducibility and the claimed computational bound.

The experimental protocol is insufficiently specified for reproduction and uncertainty assessment. Appendix B.5 acknowledges randomly sampled benchmark subsets but does not give complete sample counts, selected instances, or seeds; utility decoding parameters and maximum generation lengths are also missing. Attack experiments use only 50 AdvBench queries, and results lack confidence intervals or repeated-run estimates. Large improvements are promising, but small differences and claims of consistent superiority are less secure.

The attention-based mechanism receives suggestive rather than decisive validation. Similar marginal distributions of human and detected transition positions in Figure 3 do not establish per-example localization accuracy; annotation sample sizes and inter-annotator agreement are unreported. Figure 4 evaluates top-three agreement although deployment selects one path. Matched-compute random path selection and random or fixed-token intervention controls would better isolate the contribution of attention. Observational IAS correlations do not establish the stated sufficient condition for safety.

The robustness evidence is limited to the evaluated attacks, with no clearly documented defense-aware adaptive evaluation. Automated judges are not validated specifically for reasoning traces containing both refusals and harmful content, and AdvBench Harmfulness Rate counts only the maximum severity score. Additional human calibration and severity-sensitive reporting would strengthen the safety conclusions.

The low-cost claim rests primarily on average per-token generation time on harmful prompts. This does not establish end-to-end latency, throughput, or memory overhead under comparable attention implementations and batching. Accounting should explicitly include discarded branches, lookahead, cache rebuilding, and attention extraction. Overall, the promising empirical contribution needs important methodological and reporting revisions before a sound, reproducible Findings recommendation is justified.
